1.pericope_label: Woe to thee that spoilest, and thou wast not spoiled; and dealest treacherously, and they dealt not treacherously with thee! when thou shalt cease to spoil, thou shalt be spoiled; and when thou shalt make an end to deal treacherously, they shall deal treacherously with thee

schools.summary: Ellicott opens with the most candid structural admission in the book: no chapter in the prophet's writings presents so little traceable connection, a thought expressed in one or two verses and then another following without anything to link it on. He offers two explanations, the strong emotion which filled the prophet's mind as he looked on the coming perils of his country, or, as he thinks more probable, that we have a series of rough notes, memoranda for a long discourse afterwards delivered in a more continuous form, which would be more intelligible if printed separately, as a French moralist's fragments are printed, since the verse arrangement gives a fictitious semblance of continuity. On the occasion he is precise: the words are addressed to Sennacherib on his second campaign, undertaken without the slightest provocation, since Hezekiah had submitted and paid an enormous indemnity for the costs of the first war and had since taken no aggressive action, so that the invasion was undisguised spoliation and rapacity; for treacherously he would read rapaciously, and on such aggressiveness a righteous retribution was sure to come.

Gill reports the field before choosing: some understand Nebuchadnezzar and others Sennacherib, which he grants is more probable, while a rabbi offers a conditional, Sennacherib for Hezekiah's times but the king of nations of the vision for the Messiah's, and a later scholar applies the whole prophecy to the Maccabees. His own reading is the Roman antichrist, to whom power was given over all kindreds and tongues, the spoiler of men's substance by confiscation, their bodies by imprisonment and death, their families by persecution and other men's souls by false doctrine. Calvin hesitates openly between two enemies. If the words are expounded of the Babylonians the strain flows easily enough, since having just promised freedom to the prisoners the prophet appropriately taunts their conquerors, who needed to be peculiarly confirmed in a prediction that appeared incredible, and who amidst such distresses might have fainted and given up all hope had the prophet not met them with these exhortations. Yet because it is almost universally agreed that a new discourse begins here, addressed to Sennacherib and his army, he is not unwilling to believe it, and reads the threat as a wonderful revolution of affairs which will overthrow Nineveh, invincible as it appears, when the Babylonians come to punish that cruelty.

Clarke treats the chapter as a composition before treating it as a prophecy. It is the sequel of the Sennacherib prophecy, manifestly distinct from the foregoing and peculiarly elegant, and to set it in a proper light he marks the transitions from one part to another: the first verse addressed to the Assyrian, briefly but strongly and elegantly, on the injustice of his ambitious designs and their sudden disappointment; the second introducing the Jews offering earnest supplication in their distress; the third and fourth the prophet, or rather God himself, threatening the invader that notwithstanding the terror he had occasioned he should fall and become an easy prey to those he had intended to subdue; the fifth and sixth a chorus of Jews acknowledging the mercy and power of God. Wesley answers the question of identity in four words, Sennacherib, who wasted the land of Judah.

Henry reads the verse morally rather than historically, in three heads. The sin is that the enemy spoiled the people of God and made a prey of them, breaking his treaty of peace and dealing treacherously, and truth and mercy are so sacred, and have so much of God in them, that those who make conscience of neither cannot but be under the wrath of God: bloody and deceitful men are the worst of men. The aggravation is that he spoiled those who had never done him any injury and dealt treacherously with those who had always dealt faithfully, whence the rule that the less provocation we have from men to do a wrong thing, the more provocation we give to God by doing it. The punishment answers exactly: the army destroyed by an angel, the camp plundered by those it had preyed on, the Chaldeans revolting from the Assyrians, and two of the king's own sons murdering him at his devotions, since the righteous God often pays sinners in their own coin.

debates.question: Who is the spoiler addressed in the woe?

positions.view: Sennacherib, on his second campaign against Judah.
Nebuchadnezzar and Sennacherib are both reported, and a rabbi and a later scholar offer other names, but the Roman antichrist is meant.
The words would run more easily of the Babylonians, but he yields to the general agreement that a new discourse begins here against the Assyrian.

debates.question: Is this chapter a continuous composition?

positions.view: Its plan is peculiarly elegant and manifestly distinct from the foregoing, with transitions that can be marked verse by verse.
No chapter in the prophet presents so little traceable connection; it reads as rough notes for a discourse delivered later in continuous form.

debates.question: What is the woe meant to do for those who hear it?

positions.view: Confirm prisoners in a prediction that appeared incredible, by taunting their conquerors.
Set out a moral reckoning, since the righteous God often pays sinners in their own coin.

outliers.note: Proposes printing the chapter as detached fragments, on the analogy of a French moralist's Pensées, since the verse arrangement gives a fictitious semblance of continuity.
Declines to settle whether the enemy is Babylon or Assyria, sets out the case for Babylon at length, and then defers to the consensus.

themes: Woe to thee that spoilest, and thou wast not spoiled; and dealest treacherously, and they dealt not treacherously with thee! when thou shalt cease to spoil, thou shalt be spoiled; and when thou shalt make an end to deal treacherously, they shall deal treacherously with thee.

2.pericope_label: O LORD, be gracious unto us; we have waited for thee... At the noise of the tumult the people fled... And wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times, and strength of salvation: the fear of the LORD is his treasure

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps the shift of person and makes it evidence: in the change from their arm to our salvation we hear the very words of the prayer as it was spoken, the first referring to the soldiers who were to fight the battles of their country, the second to the non-combatants assembled with the prophet in supplication. He hears in the tumult of the following verse the rush and crash as of a mighty tempest, when God at last uplifts himself for the deliverance of his chosen; addresses the spoil to the invader, who came to spoil and should find himself spoiled, his camp stripped as caterpillars and locusts strip the green herbage; and takes the vision of the fifth verse for the ideal city of God, filled at last with judgment and righteousness. On the sixth he reads wisdom and knowledge in the higher sense, in contrast with the craft and devices of men, and the fear of the Lord as the true treasure, in contrast with the silver and gold in which Hezekiah had been led to place his trust. Delitzsch takes the arm for the power that shelters God's people, needed every morning because the danger is renewed every day, and sees the answer to the prayer while the prophet is still praying: the noise comes from God, raising himself judicially above Assyria and thundering as a judge.

Gill hears the prayer as the church's under persecution, imploring God's favour in her distress and pleading not any merits of her own but casting herself on his mercy and kindness. He reports that the Latin renders the noise of the tumult as the voice of the angel and that a father of the church passes on the Jewish opinion naming Gabriel, while others take it of the noise made in the air or in the camp when the angel smote them; has the spoil gathered as easily as the caterpillar consumes what is green, with most understanding it of the Jews going into the camp after the destruction; and prefers to read the sixth verse as an apostrophe to the Messiah, of the later times when the knowledge of him shall be increased until the earth is covered with it. Calvin marks the order the prophet follows, exhibiting the promise of God first and immediately exhorting to prayer, breaking off the stream of his discourse to do it, so that the godly may know where to go amidst such distresses. He treats the defeat as already accomplished, bidding the Jews look on the ruin of a power all men reckoned invincible as having taken place, notes the plural because the Assyrian kingdom consisted of various peoples, and raises a question the others do not, whether the passage denotes the final ruin of the nation or only the defeat before the walls of Jerusalem, which almost all commentators assume but which he finds too limited.

Clarke emends the prayer. For their arm the Syriac, the old paraphrase and the Latin all read our arm, and an early edition has the same in its margin; since the prophet is praying against the enemies of God's people, this part of the prayer cannot be in their behalf, so our arm is the true reading, though he can confirm it from none of the manuscripts he has consulted, and he quotes his own old English Bible, be thou oure arm in erly. He follows the Greek and Syriac in reading terrible for multitude in the following verse, giving from thy terrible voice, cites the same rabbi as Gill for the east, reports a word of the clause missing from a manuscript and the Syriac, and notes that a Greek translator's copy read thy treasure rather than his. Wesley smooths what Clarke emends, since the change of persons is frequent in prophetical writings; reads every morning of the hour of the morning sacrifice, comprehensively rather than exclusively, the morning being put for the whole day, so that the sense is help us speedily and continually; makes the Medes and Persians a rod in God's hand; and turns the sixth verse to Hezekiah, whose throne shall be established on the sure foundations of wisdom and justice, his chief treasure lying in promoting the fear and worship of God.

debates.question: Should the prayer read their arm or our arm?

positions.view: Keep their arm: the change of person preserves the prayer as spoken, first for the soldiers and then for the non-combatants.
Read our arm with three versions, since a prayer against the enemies cannot ask a blessing on them.
No emendation is needed; the change of persons is frequent in prophetical writings.
The arm is simply the power that shelters God's people, required afresh every morning.

debates.question: Who is addressed in the verse about the spoil?

positions.view: The invader, who came to spoil and finds himself spoiled.
The Assyrians, by a sudden turn of direct address, though the words might be referred to the Jews with the noun read actively.
The Jews, who gather the spoil of the camp after the destruction.

debates.question: Whose times are made stable by wisdom and knowledge?

positions.view: Hezekiah's: his throne established on the sure foundations of wisdom and justice.
The kingdom under a pious reign, contrasted with its ruinous state under the previous king.
The Messiah's later times, when the knowledge of him shall cover the earth.
Neither reign in particular: wisdom and knowledge stand in the higher sense against the craft and devices of men.

outliers.note: Adopts a reading he admits no manuscript he has seen supports, on the internal ground that a prayer against the enemy cannot bless the enemy.
Has the prophet see the answer while the prayer is still being made, so that the tumult of the next verse is God's own judicial thunder.

themes: O Lord, be gracious unto us; we have waited for thee: be thou their arm every morning, our salvation also in the time of trouble.
At the noise of the tumult the people fled; at the lifting up of thyself the nations were scattered.
And your spoil shall be gathered like the gathering of the caterpiller: as the running to and fro of locusts shall he run upon them.
The Lord is exalted; for he dwelleth on high: he hath filled Zion with judgment and righteousness.
And wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times, and strength of salvation: the fear of the Lord is his treasure.

7.pericope_label: Behold, their valiant ones shall cry without: the ambassadors of peace shall weep bitterly... Now will I rise, saith the LORD; now will I be exalted... And the people shall be as the burnings of lime: as thorns cut up shall they be burned in the fire

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the disputed opening word literally, their lions of God, and connects it with the lion-name given to the city in an earlier chapter, so that these are the lion-like heroes of the lion-like city, the whole passage painting the panic caused by the approach of Sennacherib. He identifies the ambassadors as the envoys sent to the Assyrian at Lachish, weeping at the hard conditions imposed, whether those on record or some yet harder demand for the surrender of the city; says no traveller dared show himself on the main road, and denounces the invader for breaking the treaty though the king had complied with his conditions; takes the four named places as types of beauty and fertility now languishing, and floats the suggestion that the embassy was sent in the autumn, so that the prophet saw the symbols of failure and decay in the natural features of the season. On the rising of God he notes the emphatic iteration of the adverb of time, man's necessity being as ever God's opportunity; reads the chaff and stubble as addressed primarily to the invaders but with a side glance at all who had woven their own webs of policy instead of trusting God; and finds limekiln and thorn-fed oven alike in leaving a residuum of ashes. Delitzsch says the noise comes from God, and takes the first simile for the totality of the destruction, so completely burned that nothing but ashes is left.

Gill follows the rabbis who read the opening word as their angels, and takes it of the angels and pastors of the churches, the two witnesses who prophesy in sackcloth and are slain and lie unburied. He reads the wasted highways of the ways of Zion, mourning because none come to the solemn feasts, none daring to attend the ministry of the word; takes the mourning earth of a later Christendom under tyranny, with the faithful witnesses slain and a stop put to all gospel ministrations; and makes the rising of God a change of posture, since he had been as one lain down and asleep, as if careless about his honour and interest, and now determines to arise and show himself strong. Calvin notes that the old paraphrase and some ancient versions treated the disputed word as a contraction meaning I will appear to them, and objects that there is no example of the shortened form. He then raises a question nobody else asks, whether the prophet relates historically the fearful perplexity and imminent danger to which the Jews were reduced, in order to exhibit the favour of deliverance more strikingly, or predicts a future calamity so that the hearts of the godly should not be caught unprepared. He adds the commercial consequence of the closed roads, insists the description is the prophet's own rather than the ambassadors' report, observes that the places named form almost the farthest boundaries of the holy land so that no part remains uninjured, and says the Lord laughs at men who think everything in their power when the slightest expression of his will can restrain them.

Clarke reports three manuscripts with a form meaning lions of God, or strong lions, an appellation for heroes which the Arabians and Persians still use, and cites the case of a warrior surnamed the lion of God for his courage and valour; he also follows the Syriac and the old paraphrase in a second word of the same verse. On the mourning land he notes only that the Greek read a different word in the last clause, giving stripped of their beauty; and on the chaff he prefers a conjecture reading my spirit for your breath, confirmed by the old paraphrase, where my word answers to my spirit. Wesley says the representation is made lively so that the promised mercy may be duly magnified, the envoys weeping because they cannot obtain their desires; explains that the Assyrian broke the faith he had given for a sum of money and contemned the fortified cities of Judah which he easily took; describes the two famous places as spoiled of their fruits; reads the conception of chaff as great hopes and designs utterly disappointed, the rage against God's people bringing ruin on themselves; and says the people shall be burnt as easily and effectually as chalk is burned to lime.

debates.question: What is the word rendered their valiant ones?

positions.view: Literally their lions of God: the lion-like heroes of the lion-like city.
Three manuscripts give a form meaning lions of God, a title for heroes still used among Arabs and Persians.
Their angels, with the rabbis: the pastors of the churches, the witnesses who prophesy in sackcloth.
The ancient versions treated it as a contraction meaning I will appear to them, but the shortened form has no parallel.
The literal roads of Judah, emptied by war, the invader having broken a treaty the king had already honoured.
The roads shut so that none go in or out and merchandise ceases; the description is the prophet's own, not a report by the ambassadors.
The ways of Zion, mourning because none come to the solemn feasts.

debates.question: What do the lime and the burning thorns signify?

positions.view: The totality of the destruction: so completely burned that nothing but ashes is left.
Limekiln and thorn-fed oven alike, whose work is seen in a residuum of ashes.
Hardness bruised, as fire softens stone until it can be reduced to powder.
Burnt as easily and effectually as chalk is burned to lime.

outliers.note: Leaves open whether the passage reports a distress already suffered or predicts one still to come, and grants that the tense will not settle it.
Supports a Hebrew reading from Arabic and Persian usage, citing a warrior surnamed the lion of God.

themes: Behold, their valiant ones shall cry without: the ambassadors of peace shall weep bitterly.
The highways lie waste, the wayfaring man ceaseth: he hath broken the covenant, he hath despised the cities, he regardeth no man.
The earth mourneth and languisheth: Lebanon is ashamed and hewn down: Sharon is like a wilderness; and Bashan and Carmel shake off their fruits.
Now will I rise, saith the Lord; now will I be exalted; now will I lift up myself.
Ye shall conceive chaff, ye shall bring forth stubble: your breath, as fire, shall devour you.
And the people shall be as the burnings of lime: as thorns cut up shall they be burned in the fire.

13.pericope_label: Hear, ye that are far off, what I have done... The sinners in Zion are afraid... Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire?... He that walketh righteously, and speaketh uprightly... he shall dwell on high

schools.summary: Delitzsch observes that while addressing Assyria the prophet does not overlook the sinners of his own nation who deserve punishment: the judgment on Assyria is an alarming lesson not only for the heathen but for Israel too, since there is no respect of persons with God. Even for the sinners in Jerusalem there is no abiding in the presence of the Almighty and Just One who has judged Assyria; they must either repent or they cannot remain, for God, so far as his wrath is concerned, is a consuming fire. He identifies the answer that follows as the prophet's own variation on two psalms, as a later prophet varies another, and notes that over the picture of the man who dwells on high the prophet forgets the sinners in Zion altogether and greets with words of promise the thriving church of the future. Ellicott says the fate of Assyria is proclaimed as a warning to other nations and to Israel itself, and that for the sinners in Zion there is the furnace of the wrath of God, whose everlasting burnings are one aspect of his righteousness.

Calvin treats the summons as a formal preface, spoken as by one about to handle a very weighty subject, and addressed both to those who would be eyewitnesses and to the most distant nations to whom the report would be communicated, so that the power of God should be perceived not by a few at hand but at a very great distance. He then puts an objection to himself: might one not say the subject is not important enough to need so lofty a preface, since it amounts only to wicked men being struck with fear? On examination it is no ordinary exhibition of divine power when wicked men are roused from their indolence so that, whether they will or not, they perceive that God is their judge; and this holds especially where contempt of God is joined to hypocrisy, since though it is hard to rouse irreligious men when a veil is spread over their hearts, greater still is the obstinacy of hypocrites, who imagine that God is under obligation to them and who set aside all prophecies by witty jesting. On the answer he says God's blessing is ready for the upright, who have no reason to dread that burning since they shall dwell in the greatest safety, whereas of slanderers and robbers who cannot restrain tongue, hands, ears and eyes we need not wonder if God is severe, since while God is their judge their own conscience is at the same time their executioner. Gill rejects the local reading of the sinners in Zion for formal professors in the reformed churches, having a form of godliness without the power, who will panic when God's judgments fall on antichrist, unless antichrist's own followers are meant; and he reads the dwelling on high of the saints by faith now, of the spiritual reign after antichrist's fall, and of the saints in heaven, safe from the everlasting burnings.

Clarke reasons from the name: Zion has generally been considered a type of the Church of God, all whose members should be holy and given to good works, so that sinners in Zion are portentous beings, and yet, he asks, where are they not? He thinks the old paraphrase of the verse worthy of notice and quotes it whole, that the sinners in Zion are broken down and fear has seized the ungodly who suffer for their ways, so that they say, who among us shall dwell in Zion where the splendour of the Divine Majesty is like a consuming fire, and who of us in Jerusalem where the ungodly are judged and delivered into hell for an eternal burning; and he adds his old English Bible's rendering, everdurynge brennyngis. On the answer he notes a manuscript variant in the clause about stopping the ears. Wesley takes the sinners plainly for the Jews, the prophet having foretold the deliverance of God's people and the destruction of their enemies and now giving a lively representation of the unbelieving condition the Jews were in before their deliverance came, asking how they should endure the wrath of a God who is a consuming fire; and he glosses the righteous man as just in all his dealings, refusing to hearken to counsels tending to shed innocent blood, abhorring the very sight of sin committed by others and guarding his eyes from occasions of sin, dwelling on high out of the reach of danger with all necessaries furnished.

Henry finds in the summons a preface that commands attention, and thinks it fit that all should attend, both near and afar off: let distant regions and future ages hear what God has done, and they will, from the scripture, with as much assurance as those who were near and those who lived at the time; but whoever hears, let them acknowledge his might, that it is irresistible, for those are very stupid who hear what God has done and yet will not acknowledge it. He finds among the sinners in Zion hypocrites who enjoy Zion's privileges and concur in Zion's services while their hearts are not right, and on the promise keeps to experience: the divine power will keep the believer safe and his faith in that power will keep him easy, he shall want nothing needful for him, and the remembrance of the terror they were in shall add to the pleasure of their deliverance.

debates.question: Who are the sinners in Zion?

positions.view: The Jews, in the unbelieving condition they were in before their deliverance came.
Hypocrites who enjoy Zion's privileges and share its services while their hearts are not right.
Members of a Church whose members ought all to be holy, which makes them portentous beings.
Formal professors in the reformed churches, or else antichrist's own followers.

debates.question: Whom does the summons to hear address?

positions.view: Both eyewitnesses and the most distant nations to whom the report would come.
Distant regions and future ages, who hear it from the scripture as surely as those who stood near.
The heathen and Israel alike, since there is no respect of persons with God.

debates.question: What are the devouring fire and the everlasting burnings?

positions.view: God himself, who so far as his wrath is concerned is a consuming fire, before whom sinners must repent or go.
One aspect of the righteousness of God.
Hell, with the old paraphrase, where the ungodly are judged and delivered to an eternal burning.

outliers.note: Objects to the passage's own importance and then answers himself, arguing that rousing hypocrites is a greater exhibition of power than rousing the openly irreligious.
Quotes the old paraphrase of the verse entire, judging it worthier of notice than his own comment.

themes: Hear, ye that are far off, what I have done; and, ye that are near, acknowledge my might.
The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?

He that walketh righteously, and speaketh uprightly; he that despiseth the gain of oppressions, that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes, that stoppeth his ears from hearing of blood, and shutteth his eyes from seeing evil;
He shall dwell on high: his place of defence shall be the munitions of rocks: bread shall be given him; his waters shall be sure.

17.pericope_label: Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off... Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities... But there the glorious LORD will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams

schools.summary: Ellicott grants that the words about the king, torn from their context, have been not unfitly used to describe the beatific vision of the saints in the far-off land of heaven, and that the old paraphrase gives thine eyes shall see the Shekinah of the King of Ages; but their primary meaning, he insists, is obviously historical. The king is Hezekiah, hitherto so deeply humiliated, seen no longer in sackcloth and ashes with downcast eyes but in all the beauty of triumph and majesty, and the land that is very far off is the whole land of Israel, prosperous and peaceful, against the narrow range of view the people had while pent up within the walls during the siege. He has the heart recall the evil days as a dream that had passed away, leaving behind the thankful joy which rises out of such recollections; names the scribe who fixed the tribute, the weigher who weighed the gold and silver, and the counter of towers who formed his plans for the siege, noting that a psalm uses the last phrase of those who defend the city; hears in the restored Zion an echo of two psalms probably written on the destruction of Sennacherib's army; and takes the broad rivers as rivers and canals, the bold imagery starting from what the prophet had heard of the great cities of the Tigris and Euphrates, since what those rivers were to Nineveh and Babylon the presence of God would be to a Jerusalem that could boast only of the softly going waters of Shiloah. Delitzsch says the dreadful past is so thoroughly forced out of mind by the glorious present that they must turn their thoughts back to remember it at all, and that the prophet passes over into the tone of the same psalm.

Gill takes the king for more than Hezekiah in his royal robes with his sackcloth put off: the King Messiah in the glory of his person and office, whom the apostles saw in the days of his flesh and whom believers now see by faith, crowned with glory and honour, and shall before long see personally. He applies the remembered terror to a later church recalling the slaying of the witnesses with gratitude for deliverance; makes the fierce people of the next verse a character of the Papists, furious in temper and bloodthirsty in practice, whose consciences are seared; and observes that Egypt had its Nile and Babylon its Euphrates while Jerusalem had no such river for commerce or defence, so that God promises to be that instead, which expresses the abundance and freeness of his grace as well as the safety of his church. Calvin connects the promise about the king with the verse before it and with the siege: when Jerusalem was besieged, the king shut up within the city and surrounded by treacherous counsellors, the people unsteady and seditious and everything hastening to ruin, there appeared to be no hope left, yet the royal authority in the family of David was a remarkable pledge of the love of God. He refuses to read the following verb as a past tense, since although the exchange of tenses is customary he believes the prophet warns of distresses still approaching rather than relating those already endured, and takes the exclamations that follow as speeches reported dramatically to express the impression made on the speakers' minds. On the fierce people he reports that some translate the word strong and others impudent, but takes it for fierceness, confirmed by the want of a shared tongue, since nothing so excites compassion as the intercourse of speech by which men explain their distresses, and where it is wanting each party is a barbarian to the other. He prefers the accusative to the vocative in the call to look upon Zion, and gives the reason for the city's stability, that a Church resembling a movable tent outlasts the best founded cities because the Lord is in the midst of her, while separated from him it would fall without any attack, consisting of men only, than whom nothing can be more weak or frail.

Clarke gives the counter of towers as the commander of the enemy's forces, who surveyed the fortifications of the city and took account of the height, strength and situation of the walls and towers in order to know where to make the assault with the greatest advantage, and quotes a passage of a Greek tragedy which a scholar had applied as an illustration of the place. He would read thou shalt see Zion with the old paraphrase, and records the Masoretic note at the end of that verse marking the middle of the book of Isaiah; and he takes the opening word of the river verse as a noun, giving the glorious name of Jehovah. Wesley takes the king in two stages, first Hezekiah and then Christ, triumphing over all enemies and ruling his own people with righteousness, and reads the land very far off as liberty to go abroad with honour and safety instead of being shut up in Jerusalem. He alone makes the three officials Judah's own: the scribe, whom we call muster-master, who was to make and keep a list of the soldiers and call them together as occasion required; the receiver, who received and laid out the money for the charges of the war; and he that counted the towers, who surveyed all the parts of the city and considered what fortifications were to be made or repaired, the people resorting to these officers with great distraction and confusion. He adds that the chief part of Zion's glory was that God was solemnly worshipped there, that the promised quiet was but imperfectly fulfilled in the literal Zion and clearly in the mystical, and that though the city had nothing but a small and contemptible brook, God would be as sure a defence as if it were surrounded with great rivers.

debates.question: Who is the king seen in his beauty?

positions.view: Hezekiah, primarily and historically, no longer in sackcloth but in the beauty of triumph.
The King Messiah, seen by the apostles in the flesh and by believers now through faith.
Both, in order: first Hezekiah, then Christ.
The Davidic king restored, whose authority was the one remaining pledge of God's love during the siege.

debates.question: Whose are the scribe, the receiver and the counter of towers?

positions.view: Assyrian: the officer who raised the tribute, the weigher of the gold and silver, and the planner of the siege.
Judah's own: the muster-master, the paymaster of the war, and the surveyor of fortifications needing repair.

debates.question: Is the terror remembered or still to come?

positions.view: Remembered: the dreadful past is so forced out by the glorious present that they must turn their thoughts back to it.
Remembered as a dream that had passed, leaving the thankful joy such recollections bring.
Still approaching: he keeps the future tense deliberately, taking the exclamations as speeches reported dramatically.
Remembered by a later church, recalling the slaying of the witnesses.

outliers.note: Alone makes the three named officials Judah's own war administration rather than the Assyrian assessors every other voice sees.
Records the Masoretic note at this verse marking the middle of the book of Isaiah.

themes: Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off.
Thine heart shall meditate terror. Where is the scribe? where is the receiver? where is he that counted the towers?
Thou shalt not see a fierce people, a people of a deeper speech than thou canst perceive; of a stammering tongue, that thou canst not understand.

Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities: thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, neither shall any of the cords thereof be broken.
But there the glorious Lord will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby.

22.pericope_label: For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us. Thy tacklings are loosed... And the inhabitant shall not say, I am sick: the people that dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity

schools.summary: Ellicott would omit the supplied verb and take the threefold iteration of the divine name, each time with a special characteristic, as the subject of the final verb. On the loosed tackling he weighs both readings, either Assyria as one of the ships that had been wrecked or Zion as a vessel driven by the wind and tossed but escaping shipwreck, and on the whole finds the first most in harmony with the context, noting that some critics have taken the terms for the cords, poles and canvas of a tent instead. The wrecked ship is plundered by those it came to plunder, and the lame, commonly excluded from a share of the spoils as incapable of active service, here have their portion. On the last verse he traces the words to the pestilence which attacked the Assyrian army and had probably been felt during the siege in Jerusalem itself, so that the prophet, seeing in such a pestilence the punishment of iniquity, couples together the two blessings of health and pardon: healthy because holy was his report of the restored city. Delitzsch supplies a page of technical rigging, on the cross plank that connects the two sides of the ship, the socket in the keel boards, the stays carried forward to the bows and the hollow into which the mast is laid on landing, so that slack stays let the mast fall backwards out of both its sockets at once; and he alone refers the wrecked vessel to Jerusalem.

Gill refers the threefold name to Christ, to whom all judgment is committed by the Father, who will judge his people, right their wrongs and avenge their injuries; takes the loosed tacklings for gear forsaken by the mariners as of no further use; and on the last verse has the inhabitant of Zion in the latter day unable to say I am sick, either with the sickness of sin, since all such diseases will be healed by the rising of the sun of righteousness with healing in his wings, or with the sickness of affliction from persecuting enemies, which will be at an end, such joy attending their deliverance that former sorrows are forgotten. Calvin makes the threefold name the definition of a church: God dwells where he is worshipped and acknowledged as lawgiver and king, so that those who obey him and yield subjection know by experience that he is the guardian of their salvation, while those who falsely glory in his name vainly hope for his assistance, and the true Church of God is that which acknowledges him as Lawgiver and King. He directs the ship to the Assyrians and in their person to all the enemies of the Church, rebuking the foolish confidence of ungodly men who imagine themselves rooted to the centre of the earth, and following out his own earlier comparison: having made the Church a fortified place surrounded by very broad rivers, he now makes her enemies ships with no solid foundation. On the last verse he says the second clause explains the first, since nothing prevents the blessings of God from being largely enjoyed once our sins have been pardoned, whence all the miseries that press upon us spring from no other source.

Clarke represents the Assyrians under the figure of a ship wrecked by a violent storm, with the people on the beach, young, old, feeble and diseased, gathering the spoil without any to hinder them; reports a rabbi who understands the whole chapter of Hezekiah and the king of Assyria, and other rabbis who apply it all to the days of the Messiah; and prefers the Syriac, Greek and Latin reading of the mast to the received text, which he finds extremely obscure. On the last verse he takes the army to be reduced by the stroke of God to so shattered and weak a condition that the Jews fall on the remnant and plunder them without resistance, the most infirm of the people of Jerusalem coming in for a share, the lame seizing the prey and even the sick throwing aside their infirmities and recovering strength enough to hasten to the general plunder; and he reads the last line as parallel to the first, since sickness is considered a visitation from God and a punishment of sin, so that the forgiveness of sin is equivalent to the removal of a disease, as in the psalm where the second line only varies the expression of the first. Wesley glosses the offices in turn, the judge to plead our cause against our enemies and the lawgiver as our chief governor, to whom it belongs to give laws and to defend his people; represents the Assyrian army as a gallant ship tossed in a tempestuous sea with her cables broken and all her tacklings loose, so that she has no benefit of masts or sails and is quickly swallowed up, leaving so many spoils behind that enough remains for the lame who come last; and promises the inhabitant not only a glorious temporal deliverance but, which is infinitely better, the pardon of all their sins.

debates.question: Whose ship has lost its tackling?

positions.view: Jerusalem's: the feminine address points to the city, and the contrast between now and then gives the most appropriate sense.
Assyria's, as most in harmony with the context, though Zion escaping shipwreck is arguable.
The Assyrians', wrecked by a violent storm while the people on the beach gather the spoil.
The Assyrians', and in their person every enemy of the Church, who has no solid foundation at all.

debates.question: Why is it the lame who take the prey?

positions.view: Because the lame, commonly excluded from the spoils as unfit for active service, here have their portion.
Because so many spoils are left behind that enough remains for those who come last.
Because even the sick throw aside their infirmities and recover strength enough to join the plunder.

debates.question: How are the sickness and the forgiveness of the last verse related?

positions.view: As parallel lines: sickness being a punishment of sin, forgiveness is equivalent to the removal of a disease.
Through the pestilence in the Assyrian camp and the city, which couples the blessings of health and pardon.
The second clause explains the first: all our miseries spring from sins not yet pardoned.
Two distinct gifts, a temporal deliverance and, infinitely better, the pardon of all their sins.

outliers.note: Interrupts the exposition for a technical account of ancient masts, stays and keel sockets drawn from a study of the ship in Homer and Hesiod.
Abandons the received text of the mast for the versions, on the ground that the Hebrew as it stands is extremely obscure.

themes: For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he will save us.
Thy tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast, they could not spread the sail: then is the prey of a great spoil divided; the lame take the prey.
And the inhabitant shall not say, I am sick: the people that dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity.
